Number Four
Saturday. 9:40 AM. The dressing room smells of liniment and nerves. Your kit is laid out like Amma does it at home: whites folded, pads on top, oar-blade on the thread around your neck.
Whole of Kuttanad is on the riverbank. Shibu put a bedsheet on the coconut trees and a projector on his auto.
Father Joseph blessed the projector.
Eat something. Don't look at the camera. Look at the ball.
COLLAR. Don't forget.
Also there are 400 people here and I am charging ₹10 for chairs. Amma's boat fund.
Send a selfie: thumbs up, fake confidence.
For the riverbank.
Put the phone away.
Look at the ball.
The warm-up game. Forty thousand empty seats, a few thousand full ones. In the press box, one denim jacket.
Twenty overs in, it goes wrong. Three wickets for eleven runs. The dressing-room door opens, and it's your turn.
Four down soon if you're not careful. Bat time. Then bat runs. Then win it.
Aryan watches from the balcony on crutches, in a team jacket that doesn't have his number on it any more. He doesn't clap when you walk out. He doesn't look away either.
Aryan walks out at five, two overs later, strapping showing above his sock. Every single he takes, he jogs like a man walking on glass.
Don't run me. Please. Just... don't run me.
"Boundaries only, then. I'll do the running."
Protect him.
"Then get off the field."
This is not a hospital.
You bat. Forty overs of it. Block, nudge, run. Twelve. Thirty. Fifty-one, and you touch your collar, and four hundred people on a riverbank in Kuttanad scream at a bedsheet.
Over forty-four. Aryan pushes to cover and sets off out of habit. Three strides. Then he goes down like a dropped bat, holding the back of his leg. Nobody touched him.
The physio runs on. Aryan leaves on a cart. The hamstring has gone completely. So has his World Cup.
You get there before the physio. You put his arm over your shoulder and walk him to the rope, slowly, while the whole ground claps.
You were right. Two days ago. You were right.
Last over. You're on 88. Thirteen to win. The bowler at the top of his mark is the fastest the hosts have.
13 off 6
The game that decides if you stay. You're on 88. Bhandari is on the balcony with his arms folded. Thirteen to win.
YOU STAY!
Four hundred people on a riverbank go mad.
SO CLOSE
The captain is already on his feet, clapping.
The last ball goes over midwicket and into a row of empty seats. A hundred, and a win. Sameer is the first one out of the dressing room.
Unpack.
Short. Agonisingly short, in the nineties. The hosts celebrate like it's the final. Sameer walks out to meet you anyway.
Nineties, in a warm-up. After coming in at eleven for three. I'll take that every day of my life.
Night. Your phone won't stop. Amma: a voice note of four hundred people singing a boat song. Shibu: a photo of a biscuit tin full of ten-rupee notes.
Check your email.
Someone leaked the selection minutes to every paper in Delhi. All nine vetoes.
It wasn't me. I swear it wasn't me.
Page one. Every paper in Delhi picked it up.
He's been on the phone to the Board president for three hours.
Are you okay?
A hundred in England. Beautiful. Your price just went up, and so did mine.
Monday is coming.
11:58 PM. A note slides under your door. Hotel paper. Neat handwriting.
"Selection meeting. 7 AM. Room 1204. Bring your kit bag. All of it. P. Bhandari."
7 AM. Bring your kit bag. All of it. Is he sending you home, or is someone sending him?
